topics.title: Introduction to Internal Environment Analysis
explain: Strategic analysis requires assessing the internal environment alongside external market factors.
Internal environment includes people, input-throughput-output processes, physical infrastructure, administrative hierarchy, and organizational culture.
It determines an organization's unique identity, values, ethics, and operational capabilities.
Unlike the external environment, internal analysis is specific to each firm based on its structure and business model.

flow.title: Components of Internal Environment
steps: Identify workforce and key stakeholders
Analyze internal operational processes
Assess physical infrastructure and space
Review administrative lines of authority
Evaluate culture, values, and ethics

topics.example: A technology company evaluating its specialized R&D infrastructure, developer talent, and collaborative culture before planning new product lines.
remember: Internal environment represents the sum total of internal factors shaping an organization's identity.
mistakes: Confusing internal environment components like corporate culture or operational processes with external factors like market demand.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an internal environment factor for an organization?
quiz.why: Organizational culture and values form part of the internal environment, whereas policies, competitors, and inflation are external.

quiz.q: Why is the internal environment considered specific to each organization?
o: It is controlled by external government agencies.
It is identical across all competitors in an industry.
It is based on the firm's unique structure, assets, and business model.
It changes only when external regulations change.
quiz.why: The internal environment is firm-specific because it depends on individual business models, resources, and administrative setups.

topics.title: Understanding Key Stakeholders & Mendelow's Matrix
explain: Stakeholders are internal or external individuals/groups with an interest in or impact on corporate strategy.
Mendelow's Matrix categorizes stakeholders by Power (influence level) and Interest (concern level).
Key Players (High Power, High Interest): Must be closely managed and fully engaged in strategic decisions.
Keep Satisfied (High Power, Low Interest): Require regular communication to keep them satisfied without over-engaging.
Keep Informed (Low Power, High Interest): Should be kept adequately informed to leverage feedback and avoid issues.
Low Priority (Low Power, Low Interest): Require minimal monitoring and low effort.

flow.title: Stakeholder Mapping with Mendelow's Matrix
steps: Identify all internal and external stakeholders
Assess stakeholder Power to influence strategy
Determine stakeholder Interest in organization outcomes
Map stakeholders into one of four matrix quadrants
Formulate customized engagement and communication strategies

topics.example: An e-commerce company treating its primary investors and CEO as Key Players, while treating media outlets as Low Priority unless regulatory issues arise.
remember: Stakeholders can shift quadrants dynamically if environmental events alter their power or interest level.
mistakes: Assuming stakeholder positions on Mendelow's Matrix are static over time.

quiz.q: According to Mendelow's Matrix, how should high power, high interest stakeholders be managed?
o: Kept informed through general newsletters only
Managed closely and fully engaged in decision-making
Consulted only when strategic conflicts arise
quiz.why: High power and high interest stakeholders are 'Key Players' who must be managed closely and actively involved in decisions.

quiz.q: What happens when a low interest regulatory body discovers non-compliance in a company?
o: Moves from Keep Satisfied to Low Priority
Moves from High Power/Low Interest to High Power/High Interest
Moves to Keep Informed quadrant with low power
Remains in the same quadrant permanently
quiz.why: Non-compliance triggers high interest in regulators, moving them into the High Power, High Interest (Key Player) quadrant.

topics.title: Strategic Drivers: Industry, Markets & Strategic Group Mapping
explain: Strategic drivers evaluate current business performance and what differentiates a firm from competitors.
Key strategic drivers include Industry & Markets, Customers, Products/Services, and Channels.
An industry groups firms based on their primary product (e.g., automotive, apparel).
A market comprises all buyers and sellers of a product/service in a given region.
Strategic Group Mapping is a analytical tool that groups rival firms pursuing similar competitive strategies along key variables.

flow.title: Procedure for Strategic Group Mapping
steps: Identify differentiating competitive variables in industry
Plot firms on a two-variable map using pairs
Assign firms sharing strategy space to same strategic group
Draw circles proportional to each group's sales revenue share

topics.example: Mapping laptop brands on a two-axis chart using consumer reputation (Y-axis) and product line range (X-axis) to identify direct competitive clusters.
remember: Map variables chosen should not be strongly correlated (e.g., do not map price against quality).
mistakes: Believing an industry contains only one strategic group when competitors pursue widely different market approaches.

quiz.q: What is a strategic group in industry analysis?
o: All companies operating in different geographic regions
Rival firms having similar competitive approaches and market positions
A group of suppliers controlling raw material prices
Firms selling completely unrelated products to same customers
quiz.why: A strategic group consists of competitors with similar strategies and market positions within the same industry.

quiz.q: What does the circle size represent on a Strategic Group Map?
o: Total employee strength of the company
Number of years the company has operated
Proportional share of total industry sales revenues
quiz.why: Circle sizes in strategic group mapping indicate the relative share of total industry sales revenues held by that group.

topics.title: Strategic Drivers: Customers, Products/Services & Channels
explain: A customer is the buyer of a product/service, while a consumer is the actual user (e.g., parents buy baby diapers; babies consume them).
Pricing targets the customer, while product design and usability must focus on consumer satisfaction.
Specific marketing strategies include Social, Augmented, Direct, Relationship, Services, Person, Place, Differential, Synchro, Concentrated, and Demarketing.
Channels consist of sales channels (selling intermediaries), product channels (physical movement), and service channels (post-sale support).
Strong distribution channels create robust competitive advantage and entry barriers against potential rivals.

flow.title: Distribution Channel Structure Analysis
steps: Identify target customer and consumer needs
Select appropriate sales channels and intermediaries
Establish logistics for product physical distribution
Set up service channels for installation and support
Evaluate channel strength to build entry barriers

topics.example: A beverage brand placing products in supermarkets, neighborhood stores, and quick-delivery apps to achieve intensive distribution coverage.
remember: Demarketing is used to temporarily or permanently reduce demand when facing overfull capacity.
mistakes: Failing to distinguish between customer (buyer) and consumer (end user) when designing value propositions.

quiz.q: Which marketing strategy aims to reduce demand temporarily during overfull capacity?
quiz.why: Demarketing reduces demand temporarily or permanently without destroying it (e.g., regulating peak traffic or crowded parks).

quiz.q: What is the primary role of a service channel?
o: Physically transporting products from warehouse to retail stores
Selling stock directly to wholesale distribution agents
Providing necessary installation and support after customer purchase
Managing social media advertising campaigns for products
quiz.why: The service channel consists of entities providing post-purchase installation, maintenance, and customer assistance.

topics.title: Building Core Competency & VRIN Framework
explain: Core competency (introduced by C.K. Prahalad & Gary Hamel) is the collective learning in an organization coordinating skills and integrating technologies.
Three conditions for core competency: Competitor Differentiation, Customer Value, and Application to Other Markets.
Capabilities become core competencies if they satisfy four VRIN criteria: Valuable, Rare, Costly to Imitate, Non-substitutable.
Valuable capabilities exploit market opportunities or avert external threats.
Rare capabilities are possessed by very few competing rivals.
Costly to imitate capabilities cannot be easily copied by competitors due to complex organizational routines or rapid R&D cycles.
Non-substitutable capabilities have no strategic equivalent resources.

flow.title: VRIN Evaluation Framework for Core Competency
steps: Assess if capability creates value for customers
Check if capability is rare among competitors
Evaluate if capability is costly or hard to imitate
Determine if capability lacks strategic substitutes
Confirm capability as sustainable core competency

topics.example: Intel's rapid R&D cycle time for microprocessors provided a first-mover advantage that was costly for competitors to imitate.
remember: A core competency must fulfill all four VRIN criteria to deliver sustainable competitive advantage.
mistakes: Assuming a single isolated skill or asset automatically constitutes an organizational core competency.

quiz.q: Who advocated the concept of core competency in management theory?
quiz.why: C.K. Prahalad and Gary Hamel advocated core competency as collective learning coordinating skills and integrating technologies.

quiz.q: Which criterion of VRIN ensures a capability has no equivalent strategic resource?
quiz.why: Non-substitutable capabilities have no strategic equivalents that rivals can use to achieve the same result.

topics.title: Combining External and Internal Analysis (SWOT Analysis)
explain: SWOT Analysis combines internal environment factors (Strengths, Weaknesses) with external environment factors (Opportunities, Threats).
Strength: An inherent internal capability giving a firm strategic advantage over competitors.
Weakness: An inherent internal constraint creating strategic disadvantage for the firm.
Opportunity: A favorable external condition enabling a firm to strengthen its position.
Threat: An unfavorable external condition creating risk or damage to the firm's position.
SWOT helps craft business models to leverage strengths and opportunities while overcoming weaknesses and neutralizing threats.

flow.title: SWOT Analysis Implementation Framework
steps: Identify internal strengths and competitive advantages
Pinpoint internal weaknesses and resource constraints
Scan external market opportunities for expansion
Highlight external threats from rivals and macro environment
Formulate strategic choices matching internal abilities to external market

topics.example: A law firm assessing its 70-year brand value (Strength), lack of software automation (Weakness), legal tech startups market (Opportunity), and AI legal software (Threat).
remember: Strengths and Weaknesses are internal; Opportunities and Threats are external.
mistakes: Treating SWOT as a standalone strategy decision rather than a starting framework for comparative analysis.

quiz.q: In SWOT analysis, internal factors consist of:
quiz.why: Strengths and Weaknesses originate internally, whereas Opportunities and Threats stem from the external environment.

quiz.q: What is the primary objective of performing a SWOT analysis?
o: To build full awareness of internal and external decision factors
To eliminate all market competitors immediately
To focus solely on internal operational inefficiencies
quiz.why: SWOT analysis aims to provide complete awareness of internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats for business decisions.

topics.title: Competitive Advantage & Porter's Generic Strategies: Cost Leadership
explain: Competitive advantage occurs when a firm achieves higher profitability than the industry average.
Sustainability of competitive advantage depends on Durability, Transferability, Imitability, and Appropriability.
Michael Porter identified three base generic strategies: Cost Leadership, Differentiation, and Focus.
Cost Leadership aims to produce standardized products at a very low per-unit cost for price-sensitive broad mass markets.
Achieved through demand forecasting, capacity utilization, economies of scale, standardized production, and cost-saving technology.

flow.title: Achieving Cost Leadership Strategy
steps: Forecast product demand accurately
Optimize resource utilization and scale economies
Standardize product design for mass production
Invest in advanced cost-saving technologies
Maintain strict overhead controls and minimize waste

topics.example: McDonald's using standardized food production processes and high-volume operations to maintain low unit costs.
remember: Cost leadership targets a broad market using low per-unit cost production.
mistakes: Confusing cost leadership (low cost of production) with simply setting low retail prices without internal efficiency.

quiz.q: Which characteristic determines the rate at which a firm's competitive advantage resource deteriorates over time?
quiz.why: Durability refers to the period over which a competitive advantage is sustained before resources deteriorate or become obsolete.

quiz.q: Cost Leadership Strategy is most effective when:
o: The market consists of many price-sensitive buyers
Products are highly customized for small niche markets
quiz.why: Cost leadership works best in mass markets with price-sensitive buyers where standardization yields cost savings.

topics.title: Differentiation, Focus & Best-Cost Provider Strategies
explain: Differentiation Strategy targets broad markets by offering unique product/service features valued by price-insensitive consumers.
Bases of differentiation include Product features, Premium pricing, and Organizational brand loyalty.
Focus Strategies target a narrow market segment via Focused Cost Leadership or Focused Differentiation.
Focused Cost Leadership competes on low relative price within a narrow target market.
Focused Differentiation offers unique features tailored specifically to a narrow market segment.
Best-Cost Provider Strategy combines low cost with upscale product attributes to deliver superior value compared to rivals.

flow.title: Generic Strategy Selection Logic
steps: Define Market Scope (Broad Mass Market vs Narrow Niche)
Determine Advantage Source (Low Cost vs Product Uniqueness)
Combine Broad Scope + Low Cost for Cost Leadership
Combine Broad Scope + Uniqueness for Differentiation
Target Narrow Niche for Focused Strategies or combine low cost + upscale value for Best-Cost

topics.example: Rolls-Royce applying Focused Differentiation for custom luxury cars, while smartphone makers like OnePlus offer Best-Cost Provider strategy by matching premium specs at moderate prices.
remember: Focused strategies always target a narrow buyer segment or niche market.
mistakes: Assuming differentiation strategy guarantees success even if customers do not value the differentiating features.

quiz.q: Which strategy targets a narrow market segment by offering custom unique features at premium prices?
quiz.why: Focused differentiation targets a narrow niche market with highly unique, custom product features.

quiz.q: How does a Best-Cost Provider Strategy create competitive advantage?
o: By offering inferior products at rock-bottom prices
By giving customers more value by combining lower costs with upscale features
By targeting only ultra-wealthy customers exclusively
By avoiding all research and development expenditure
quiz.why: Best-cost provider strategy gives customers superior value by emphasizing both low cost and upscale product features relative to rivals.
